steps.label: Weight sharing and transformation invariance
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp12 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 9 pages; this unit is self-study and is not taught in class; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Local sharing
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP12, a self-study unit. Prerequisites: weighted scoring with a bias (KP06), the chain rule (KP06), and using row i, column j to point at one cell of an array. We want the same object to stay in its class after it moves, which does not mean every number in the network must stay the same. The method has two steps: first restrict each unit to a small patch, a 3×3 window called the receptive field; then let every position use the same set of weights, called weight sharing. Setup: a 6×6 image with a single three-cell vertical stroke in column 1, rows 1 to 3; shifting it two columns right gives Tx with the stroke in column 3; the window moves one cell at a time with no padding, giving 4 times 4, that is 16 positions. The shared kernel K has ones in its middle column and the window in the figure scores 1 plus 1 plus 1, which is 3 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the feature maps and equivariance.

steps.label: CNN vs flatten
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the local sharing rule. This page is a BEFORE/AFTER comparison of why we share. Left: a 4×4 image flattened into a 1×16 vector feeding a fully connected layer; the top-left red cell and the bottom-right blue cell look equally far to the network, so local patterns like edges and textures cannot be learned. Right: slide one 3×3 kernel over the 2D grid: sparse (neighbours only) plus shared (one set for the whole image), so space is kept. Three benefits: far fewer parameters, a built-in local-pattern prior, and shift equivariance (shift the input one cell and the feature map shifts one cell; this is not the shift invariance that pooling gives later). Conclusion: a CNN is a special case of a fully connected layer with sparse links and weight sharing switched on; it is not magic, flatten simply throws away the 2D neighbour relation. Cells and links in the figure are schematic, not textbook size.

steps.label: Feature maps
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on CNN vs flatten. This page slides the kernel over the whole image. A feature map arranges the window scores by position, written F(x), 4×4 here. Computed cell by cell, column 0 of F(x) is 2, 3, 2, 1 and the rest are 0; column 2 of F(Tx) is 2, 3, 2, 1. The 2, 3, 2, 1 come from how many cells the window rows overlap with stroke rows 1 to 3. Translation equivariance means that shifting the input shifts the output correspondingly, F(Tx) equals T F(x). Global max pooling keeps only the maximum, z equal to max F(x), which is 3 before and after the shift: a response that moves with the stroke is equivariant and a read-out that does not depend on position is invariant. Limits: integer shifts, stride, padding and boundaries must agree, and pooling discards position (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the parameter count.

steps.label: Parameter count
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the feature maps and equivariance. This page counts parameters. Without sharing: 16 positions, each with 9 weights and 1 bias, 16 times (9 plus 1) equals 160. With sharing: all positions share 9 weights and 1 bias, 9 plus 1 equals 10. What sharing saves is the number of independently adjustable values, not the computation at each position: all sixteen positions are still computed once. The saving requires that the sharing assumption suits the task; fewer parameters do not mean more accuracy on every problem, nor that the number of operations falls to a tenth (computed by program). Next, the next page covers updating the shared weight.

steps.label: Shared update
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the parameter count. This page shows how the shared weight is updated, step by step. Let one shared weight be k; the score at position p is rp and the input multiplied by k is xp, so with local linear scoring the derivative of rp with respect to k is xp. Let δp equal the derivative of J with respect to rp; the chain rule adds up all paths: the derivative of J with respect to k equals the sum over positions of δp times xp. Numerical example: two positions give 0.2 times 3 and minus 0.1 times 1, a total gradient of 0.6 minus 0.1 equal to 0.5. With learning rate η equal to 0.1 and old k equal to 1 the update is k equal to 1 minus 0.1 times 0.5, which is 0.95, and every position then uses 0.95. The derivative of an activation is already inside δ and must be neither dropped nor repeated (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the three routes to invariance.

steps.label: Three routes
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on updating the shared weight. This page compares the three routes to invariance. Local sharing is only one architectural prior; real systems can combine the three, but first decide whether the transformation preserves the class. Choosing invariant features: first turn the data into a representation insensitive to the given transformation; the risk is losing information needed for recognition. Architectural constraints: shared weights plus a suitable pooling explicitly force some computations to be identical; the risk is that it holds only for compatible transformations. Data augmentation: generate more training examples with reasonable transformations; the risk is that finite examples usually do not guarantee invariance under every transformation. Next, the next page covers geometric sharing of pixel products.

steps.label: Geometric sharing
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the three routes to invariance. This page looks at geometric sharing in higher-order input products. The score of a higher-order network contains input products, for example v equal to b plus the sum of ai xi plus the sum of cjk xj xk, then an activation f(v). Multiplying two pixels brings the geometric relation of a pair of positions into the model. Under translation both endpoints move by t and the difference vector stays: (pk plus t) minus (pj plus t) equals pk minus pj, so the pairs that can share a coefficient are those with the same displacement vector; in the left chart both blue lines have displacement (1,1) and can share, while the orange line has displacement (2,2): same slope but no sharing, so same slope is too crude a condition. Rotation preserves segment length, so (1,0) and (0,1) both have length 1, and pairs of equal length can share a second-order coefficient. On a finite pixel grid an arbitrary rotation often needs interpolation or cropping, and exact invariance needs compatible transformations, terms and pooling. Next, the next page covers the square-term case.

steps.label: Square-term case
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on geometric sharing of pixel products. This page looks at the square-term special case. The model v equals b plus the sum of ai xi plus c times the sum of all xi squared; c is one coefficient shared by all square terms, one extra parameter rather than one per cell. The sum of squares is the squared norm of x: (1,0) and (0,1) both give 1 squared plus 0 squared equal to 1, so the sum of squares itself is invariant under orthogonal rotation. But the linear term can differ: if a equals (1,0), the scores of the two points are b plus 1 plus c and b plus c, not equal. The historical architecture: the source describes three hidden layers, the first two made of feature maps; each unit sees only a local window of the previous layer and corresponding connections on one map share weights. This is the same sharing principle as the three-cell stroke of this example but not the same architecture; without enough original detail its full parameter count or accuracy cannot be derived (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the square-term case. Two exercises. Q1: with an 8×8 input, a 3×3 window, stride 1, no padding and a shared bias, how large is the feature map and how many parameters with and without sharing? In each direction 8 minus 3 plus 1 equals 6 positions, 6 times 6 equals 36, so the map is 6×6; without sharing 36 times (9 plus 1) equals 360 and with sharing 9 plus 1 equals 10; a larger image only adds uses, not shared parameters. Q2: after sharing, the high-score position moves with the input; is that equivariance or invariance? Compare F(Tx) equal to T F(x) with F(Tx) equal to F(x): the high-score position moves, so it is equivariance; only with a suitable pooling and the conditions satisfied can invariant features arise, and in this example z is 3 after max pooling (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exact formula and boundaries.

steps.label: Exact formula
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the exercises. This is the extension: the exact shared-window formula, boundaries and the gradient. Let the image be x, the kernel K and the bias b, using cross-correlation, where the kernel is not flipped: r_ij equals b plus the sum over a and c from 0 to 2 of K_ac times x at (i plus a, j plus c); i, j is the top-left corner of the window and a, c are the row and column offsets inside the kernel, with c used to avoid a clash with the bias b. With a pointwise activation φ the feature map can be F(x)_ij equal to φ(r_ij); the main example uses the score r directly. Boundaries of a finite grid: the equivariance formula needs all corresponding positions to be valid; when an object leaves the frame, the padding differs, or the shift is incompatible with the stride, the equality may hold only in the interior; image rotation may also need interpolation, and grouping weights of equal length alone cannot remove sampling error. The shared gradient: the derivative of J with respect to k equals the sum over positions of the derivative of J with respect to r_p times the derivative of r_p with respect to k, and under local linear scoring the second factor is the input x_p at that position. That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
